newsitem.title: USA: New Jersey says fiscal 1997 surplus at $550 mln.
newsitem.headline: New Jersey says fiscal 1997 surplus at $550 mln.

text.p: New Jersey's surplus for fiscal 1997 is currently running at $550 million, with stronger-than-expected revenues contributing to the windfall, state officials said Tuesday.

State Treasurer Brian Clymer is set to review more details of New Jersey's cash position in legislative testimony Wednesday, but treasury officials offered a preview of the figures in an interview Tuesday.
Revenues collected in the first 10-months of the year totaled $13.2 billion, or about $167 million more than the state originally forecast.
Clymer said income taxes and corporate businesses taxes were showing particular strength.

Although the figures are clearly good news for New Jersey, they also mean Clymer and Gov. Christine Whitman will be on the defensive with the Legislature over Whitman's plan to borrow $2.8 billion of pension bonds.
Whitman wants to borrow the money to pay off the state's $4.2 billion unfunded pension liability, freeing up almost $600 million in budget savings with the maneuver.
But state lawmakers, balking at the unprecedented size of the proposed borrowing, have said part of the large surplus could be used to help balance the budget instead.

New Jersey earlier this year selected Merrill Lynch & Co. to underwrite the deal if it wins legislative approval. If issued in a single sale, the taxable pension bonds would be the largest deal ever in the municipal bond market.
In a statement breaking down the state's revenue collections so far this year, Clymer said April results were "especially strong," with $2 billion of revenues.

The income tax generated more than $4.1 billion for the period, $100 million above forecasts, and corporate business taxes totaled more than $1.1 billion, 13 percent higher than revised expectations. Lottery collections were $522 million, or $15.8 million below projections.
Clymer said sales tax collections were roughly on target for the period.
